# AI Workforce OS

> AI Workforce OS is a web app that gives a business its own team of AI assistants: they draft emails, sort customer questions, prepare reports and keep routine work moving, and nothing is sent or deleted until a person approves it.

The demos on these pages are simulated in your browser. Nothing is sent, and no account is needed.

## Home page (https://ai-workforce.bitecodes.com/)

AI employees for your business. Hand the busywork to AI. Keep the final say.

AI Workforce OS gives your business a team of AI assistants that draft emails, sort customer questions, prepare reports and keep routine work moving. You ask in plain words, and nothing is sent or deleted until a person says yes.

### Up and running in three steps

1. Choose your assistants: Start with ready-made assistants for HR, customer support, research and engineering, or brief a new one the way you would brief a new hire.
2. Ask in plain words: Type or say what you need. The right assistant picks it up, and passes it to a colleague when the job needs more than one.
3. Approve what matters: Emails, messages and deletions wait for your yes. Approve in one click, or let the request expire and nothing is sent.

Example requests, and what happens to each:

- "Draft the welcome email for our new starter": HR picks this up. Reads the offer and drafts the email. Sending it waits for your yes.
- "Sum up the open pull requests": Engineering Manager picks this up. Reads the pull requests and writes the summary. Posting it to Slack waits for your yes.
- "What do our documents say about pricing?": Research picks this up. Reads your files and names the source of each point. It writes a new document, and has no way to share it.
- "Reply to the overnight customer emails": Customer Support picks this up. Drafts each reply from your support handbook. Each reply waits for your yes before it is sent.

### Example assistants for the work your team repeats

- HR (hiring and onboarding): Checks applications against the role, drafts the welcome email and books interviews in the calendar.
  - Gmail: Reads and drafts emails on its own. Sending one waits for approval.
  - Calendar: Adds events to the calendar on its own. Deleting one waits for approval.
- Engineering Manager (keeping projects on track): Keeps tickets up to date, sums up open pull requests and writes the daily standup note, so nobody has to.
  - GitHub: Reads pull requests to sum them up, and opens or updates issues on its own.
  - Jira: Updates tickets on its own.
  - Slack: Reads channels on its own. Posting a message waits for approval.
- Research (market and competitor research): Pulls together what your own documents already say, points out what is missing and writes the summary into a new document.
  - Drive: Reads files and creates new documents. It has no way to share them.
- Customer Support (answering customers): Sorts the overnight queue, drafts replies from your support handbook and passes on anything it cannot answer.
  - Gmail: Drafts every reply from your handbook. Each one waits for approval before it is sent.
  - Slack: Posting a message waits for approval.

These are the example assistants of the demo workspace, whose tools use practice data.

### Built so you stay in charge

- Nothing is sent without a yes: Sending an email, posting a message or deleting something waits for a person who is allowed to approve it.
- Everyone sees only their part: Five ready-made roles, from owner to viewer, decide who can ask, who can approve and who can only look. You can make your own.
- A record you can trust: Every approval decision and every finished job is written down against the person responsible, in a record built so that a changed entry can be detected.
- Answers you can check: Answers point to the page they came from. When your documents do not cover a question, it says so instead of guessing.
- Never stuck on one AI provider: Works with 7 AI providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Gemini. If one is busy, it moves on to the next.
- Routine work on a schedule: Set a timetable in plain words, such as every weekday at 9am, and pause it whenever you like.

Who can do what, in the five built-in roles every workspace starts with (owners and admins can create roles of their own):

- Ask the AI team for work: Owner, Admin, Manager and Employee
- See the work as it happens: Owner, Admin, Manager, Employee and Viewer
- Approve what gets sent: Owner, Admin and Manager
- Change how the assistants work: Owner, Admin and Manager
- Invite people and set their roles: Owner and Admin

### What people ask before they start

#### Who is it for?

Companies that want AI assistants to take on routine work, such as hiring and onboarding, customer emails, research summaries and project updates, while people keep the final say.

#### Will it send anything without asking?

No. Sending an email, posting a message or deleting something always waits for a person who is allowed to approve it. If nobody answers before the deadline, the request expires and nothing is sent.

#### What can it do without asking?

Reading, drafting and routine updates, such as adding a calendar event or updating a ticket, happen on their own. Sending an email, posting a message and deleting something wait for a person. Owners and admins can make more actions wait for approval.

#### Do I need technical skills to use it?

No. You ask for work in plain words in Chat, typed or spoken. The one-off set-up, such as choosing which AI provider to use, is done once by whoever looks after your workspace.

#### What happens when it does not know something?

It tells you. Answers come from the documents you add, with the page each point came from. When nothing in your documents covers the question, it says it cannot answer rather than guessing.

#### Can we try it before connecting anything?

Yes. Out of the box it runs on a built-in sandbox model that gives practice answers, clearly labelled as such, and every connector works with practice data, so nothing real is sent.

#### Which AI does it use?

The one you choose: OpenRouter, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Anthropic and OpenAI. You set the order, and if one is busy or unavailable it moves on to the next.

#### Does it work with our email and calendar?

Yes. Gmail, Google Calendar, Microsoft Outlook and the other connectors connect to your real accounts once an owner or admin sets them up. Until then they use practice data, so nothing real is sent. Your IT team will find the technical details on the page for IT teams.

#### Who can see and approve things?

Each person gets a role. An employee can hand work to the AI team but cannot approve what it sends, and a viewer can look at reports but change nothing. Owners and admins can create roles of their own to fit your team.

#### How do we get started?

Create your workspace. Whoever creates it becomes the owner, can start with ready-made assistants and can invite everyone else afterwards.

## Security and technical details (https://ai-workforce.bitecodes.com/trust)

For IT and security teams: how it keeps agents in check.

The detail behind the promises on the overview: the approval gate, provider failover, the tamper-evident audit chain, cited retrieval, the permission model and what actually runs.

Agent traces are kept for 180 days by default; administrators can change this. An approval nobody decides expires after 24 hours, and nothing is sent.

Provider keys and connector credentials are stored encrypted, each under its own data key and bound to its workspace. A workspace can also require that someone other than the person who asked approves, either for every approval or only for actions that delete something or cannot be undone, such as refunds and cancellations; this is off by default.

### Permissions of each role

- Owner: Everything, and the only role that can add or remove owners.
- Admin: Everything except adding, changing or removing owners and reading other people's private conversations.
- Manager: Runs agents, approves actions, cancels runs and tasks, and edits agents. Cannot change who may.
- Employee: Asks questions in chat and hands routine work to agents. Can see approvals, cannot decide them.
- Viewer: Reads dashboards and traces. Changes nothing.

### What is actually running

- 8 independent services.
- 7 model providers (OpenRouter, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Anthropic and OpenAI), plus the offline sandbox model.
- 20 connectors (GitHub, Slack, Notion, Linear, HubSpot, Webhook, Jira, Confluence, Asana, Zendesk, Stripe, Zoom, Twilio, Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Google Sheets, Microsoft Outlook, Microsoft Teams and Salesforce). All of them connect live once an administrator adds a token or signs in with the provider, and use practice data until then.
- 47 permission codes, composed into roles.
- 5 built-in roles, plus any roles a workspace composes.

### What it does not do

1. Agents are not autonomous. They stop at every outbound or destructive action and wait for a person.
2. Answers are only as good as the documents you connect. With nothing indexed, an agent will tell you it cannot answer.
3. The offline model is a placeholder. It returns sensible-looking text so the platform can be tried, and says so wherever it answers.
4. Each connector reaches a real account only once an administrator adds its access token or signs in with the provider (GitHub, Slack, Notion, Linear, HubSpot, webhooks, Jira, Confluence, Asana, Zendesk, Stripe, Zoom, Twilio, Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Google Sheets, Microsoft Outlook, Microsoft Teams and Salesforce). Until then agents work with practice data and nothing is sent.
